title: Quantifying Coherence-to-Entanglement Conversion Efficiency under Noisy Operations
authors: Asad Ali, H. Kuniyil, M. I. Hussain, M. T. Rahim, Abdallah Slaoui, Saif Al-Kuwari
abstract: We investigate the noise-limited conversion of local quantum coherence into bipartite entanglement in a minimal two-qubit protocol comprising a coherent single-qubit input, an incoherent ancilla, an ideal CNOT operation, and subsequent environmental noise. Employing the $l_1$-norm of coherence and the entanglement negativity as resource quantifiers, we establish an exact closed-form correspondence between local single-qubit input coherence and the two-qubit entanglement generated in the noiseless limit, showing that the output negativity is precisely one half of the initial $l_1$-coherence. We then derive analytic expressions for the surviving entanglement and the associated coherence-to-entanglement conversion efficiency under two representative noise mechanisms: independent phase damping and global two-qubit depolarizing noise. The two channels exhibit qualitatively distinct degradation behavior. Phase damping induces a universal multiplicative suppression of the generated entanglement, yielding a coherence-independent conversion efficiency and no finite-noise entanglement sudden death. In contrast, global depolarization introduces an isotropic mixing contribution that shifts the partial-transpose spectrum, producing coherence-dependent degradation and a finite sudden-death threshold. We show that maximally coherent inputs not only maximize the entanglement generated by the CNOT protocol but also optimize its robustness against depolarizing noise. Direct density-matrix simulations validate the analytic results to numerical precision. These findings provide a compact analytic benchmark for assessing how different noise mechanisms constrain coherence-to-entanglement conversion in elementary quantum-information protocols and near-term quantum devices.
summary: The paper analytically investigates the trade-off between initial local quantum coherence and generated bipartite entanglement when environmental noise is present. It compares two distinct noise channels—phase damping and global depolarization—showing that they induce fundamentally different decay mechanisms. The findings establish key thresholds for entanglement sudden death, providing vital guidelines for assessing hardware performance in quantum computing protocols.
main_problem: The study quantifies how efficiently local quantum coherence can be converted into bipartite entanglement when the system is subjected to environmental noise.
main_result: Different noise channels (phase damping vs. global depolarization) cause distinct degradation patterns, with one leading to a finite threshold for entanglement sudden death while the other causes smooth multiplicative decay.
method: The authors use analytical derivations and numerical simulations based on calculating the entanglement negativity via the partial transpose spectrum of the density matrix.
model_or_system: The model is a minimal two-qubit protocol involving an initial coherent single-qubit input, followed by an ideal CNOT gate, and subsequent environmental noise modeled by specific CPTP maps (phase damping or global depolarizing noise).
key_observables: Entanglement Negativity ($N$), Coherence-to-Entanglement Conversion Efficiency ($\eta$), and the critical noise strength for Entanglement Sudden Death ($p_c$).
important_parameters: Input coherence angle $	heta$ (determining $C_{l1} = \sin(2	heta)$) and noise parameters ($p$ for damping or depolarization).
main_assumptions: The analysis is restricted to the X-state structure generated by the CNOT protocol, and the comparison focuses on negativity as the entanglement measure.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the decay of negativity versus noise strength ($p$) for both noise types, showing phase damping vanishing at $p=1$ and global depolarization vanishing at a finite threshold $p_c(	heta)$.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the ideal noiseless conversion rate ($	ext{Negativity} =  rac{1}{2} C_{l1}$), then deriving analytic expressions for entanglement under phase damping, followed by analyzing global depolarization, and concluding with a direct comparison of the resulting efficiency functions.
why_interesting: This work provides an analytical benchmark for understanding how specific noise models constrain fundamental quantum information processes like coherence-to-entanglement conversion, which is crucial for designing robust near-term quantum devices.
